speaker: Brian Potter
title: Construction Physics Author Brian Potter - Why America Struggles to Build
question: In residential construction, why can't homebuilders standardize on a handful of designs and mass-produce homes in mega-factories like automakers do?
guest: Homes are different, and a lot of that is dictated by site constraints—whether there's a hill, trees, water, different plot sizes, or where the utilities come in. So there's only so much you can make uniform just by the nature of building in a specific place with specific requirements. On top of that, there's only so far you can ship this stuff economically because it's so big and bulky. A car factory produces hundreds of thousands or millions of cars a year, but it's pretty hard to get more than a couple thousand home units out of a single housing factory. Even for really repetitive manufactured or mobile homes, factories tend to be small scale. Big manufacturers don't build everything in one mega-factory in Nevada; they run 20 facilities scattered across the country, each making a relatively small number of homes, because these factories have a catchment area of only a few hundred miles. Within those few hundred miles, you have different demands for kinds of housing, different customers who can afford different things, and different plots, so uniformity gets whittled down pretty quickly.

points.core: Site-specific physical constraints limit how uniform finished homes can ever be.
points.note: Accept: topography/hills, trees, water/drainage, varying lot sizes, or utility hookup locations forcing customization. Do not credit: vague claims that architects or buyers simply dislike uniformity.

points.note: Accept: high transport costs or physical size/weight limits restricting delivery to a regional catchment area (~100-500 miles). Do not credit: generic references to supply chain issues without the geographic shipping-radius constraint.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
They can, technically, and many have tried, but the economics rarely work because houses differ from cars in ways that erase the factory's advantages.

First, transport: a car ships cheaply across the world, while a house or its modules are bulky, mostly air, and expensive to move more than a few hundred miles. That limits each factory to a regional market, which caps the scale needed to pay off heavy automation.

Second, demand is volatile. Housing starts swing wildly with interest rates, and a factory carries high fixed costs through the busts, whereas site builders simply lay off subcontractors. This is what sank ventures like Katerra.

Third, the product isn't standard. Building codes, zoning, permitting, climate, soil and lot shapes vary by jurisdiction and by parcel, and buyers want customization.

Fourth, much of the cost never enters the factory: land, foundations, utility hookups, site work and permitting all remain local.

Finally, conventional stick-framing is already quite efficient, using cheap materials and flexible labor, so factory savings are small.

Factory building does succeed in narrower forms: manufactured homes, panels and trusses, and in Sweden and Japan.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Unlike cars, which meet uniform national standards and travel easily on trailers, houses are massive, site-bound structures governed by hyper-local realities. Physically, finished modules consist mostly of empty rooms, meaning builders must pay to ship bulky, oversized loads of air. Steep transport costs restrict a factory’s delivery radius to a few hundred miles, preventing national scale. Within that radius, standardization is thwarted by buyers expecting customization, irregular lot shapes, and thousands of municipal zoning laws and building codes covering local wind, snow, and seismic loads, plus inspectors reluctant to approve sealed factory walls. Even when standardized, modules still require custom site grading, foundations, utility hookups, and costly crane installation, leaving a large share of construction expenses outside the factory. Finally, housing demand is notoriously cyclical. Traditional builders survive downturns using flexible subcontractors and minimal fixed assets, whereas a mega-factory carries heavy capital overhead; when regional construction inevitably slows, an underutilized plant rapidly bleeds cash, erasing its assembly-line savings.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mainly because a house isn't like a car in the ways that make mass production pay off.

A house is huge, heavy, mostly empty space, and permanently attached to one piece of land. Shipping finished modules is expensive and limited by road-width rules, so a factory can only serve a few hundred miles around it. That keeps each plant's market small. Cars, by contrast, ship cheaply around the world.

A lot of the cost also can't be moved into a factory. Land, foundations, utility hookups, grading, permits and finish work happen on site and often make up half or more of the price. Even a perfect factory can only cut costs on the part it builds.

Building codes, zoning rules and climate needs differ from place to place, so it's hard to settle on a few designs. Buyers also want homes that suit their lot and neighborhood.

Housing demand rises and falls sharply with interest rates. Factories have high fixed costs and need steady output, while traditional builders using subcontractors can scale down cheaply. That mismatch is a big reason well-funded attempts like Katerra (2021) and Veev (2023) collapsed.

Factory-built homes still exist. Manufactured homes are built to one national HUD code, which avoids the local-code problem, and they make up roughly a tenth of new U.S. single-family homes.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Mass-producing homes like cars breaks down because of transportation limits, fragmented regulations, site variability, and market cyclicality. Unlike cars, which can be shipped globally from a single plant, homes are too bulky and fragile to transport far; highway size restrictions and freight costs confine factory-built housing to a small regional radius, making mega-factories uneconomical. Furthermore, while automakers design to uniform national standards, homebuilders must navigate thousands of local zoning laws, building codes, and permitting regimes that vary from town to town and often resist standardized designs. Every house also sits on a unique parcel with distinct soil conditions, topography, climate demands, and utility connections, meaning substantial site-specific engineering and foundation work must still happen on location. Finally, housing demand is fiercely cyclical and sensitive to interest rates. Traditional builders survive downturns by scaling back flexible networks of subcontractors, whereas automated mega-factories carry enormous fixed capital costs that quickly become unsustainable when the housing market slows—a dynamic that has repeatedly bankrupted industrialized housing startups.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Homebuilders can, and many already do. Subdivision builders repeat floor plans, and manufactured and modular home companies build homes on assembly lines. The challenge is getting enough orders for the same designs within economical shipping distance to keep a mega-factory busy.

A car can be shipped nationwide and driven off the lot. A home has to fit a particular lot, comply with local zoning and building rules, and be installed on a foundation with utility hookups. Shipping whole rooms also means paying to move a lot of empty space, often in oversized loads. Factories can standardize walls, floor assemblies, or entire modules, but much of the work still happens on site.

A mega-factory also has high fixed costs. If local projects stall over permits or housing demand falls, the factory still has to pay for its equipment and staff. Standardizing components or repeating plans across a subdivision captures some of the same savings without requiring a steady stream of identical homes.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Homebuilders already standardize where they can. A subdivision may use a handful of floor plans, and factories produce everything from roof trusses to entire homes. The difference is that a car leaves the factory ready to use, while a house still has to fit a particular piece of land.

Even with an identical floor plan, the slope, soil, and utility connections can change the work each lot requires. Zoning may limit what fits, and local codes may call for designs that withstand earthquakes, high winds, or heavy snow. Factories can accommodate those variations, but they need a steady stream of orders to cover their fixed costs. Cars can draw buyers from across the country. Finished house modules are bulky and expensive to ship, so a housing factory typically depends on a smaller regional market.

That makes repetition economical at a different scale. Builders can reuse plans, factory-produce parts that travel efficiently, and move crews from lot to lot.
